text.text: Nonetheless, simulated responses generated by the best-fitting models closely matched the observed mean response patterns (Fig. 6A, B).
text.formatted: Nonetheless, simulated responses generated by the best-fitting models closely matched the observed mean response patterns (Fig. <ref type="figure">6A</ref>, <ref type="figure">B</ref>).

text.text: These findings shed light on the alternative route to inference in younger children.
There has been a long-standing interest in understanding generalization in both animals and humans, with recent efforts seeking to integrate diverse conceptualizations of this capacity 1, 56, 57 .
text.formatted: There has been a long-standing interest in understanding generalization in both animals and humans, with recent efforts seeking to integrate diverse conceptualizations of this capacity <ref type="bibr">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">56,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">57</ref> .

text.text: In this study, we examined the development of generalization by (1) assessing age-related differences across several tasks, (2) testing whether inter-individual differences in performance were correlated across tasks in early and middle childhood, and (3) probing the link between memory and generalization in two inference tasks.
Four key findings emerged.
First, remembering directly learned associations benefitted both inference tasks, but performance was not correlated between them, and response patterns differed for direct versus inference pairs.

Although both tasks are often assumed to rely on a similar mechanism 4 , our data revealed only a weak association, even after reliability disattenuation, potentially reflecting distinct underlying processes.
text.formatted: Although both tasks are often assumed to rely on a similar mechanism <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">4</ref> , our data revealed only a weak association, even after reliability disattenuation, potentially reflecting distinct underlying processes.

text.text: Notably, accuracy was higher for direct pairs in the AI task, while the reverse was true for the TI task, further underscoring their potential mechanistic differences.
From a neurocomputational perspective, both tasks can be solved by the mechanism proposed in REMERGE 31 .
text.formatted: From a neurocomputational perspective, both tasks can be solved by the mechanism proposed in REMERGE <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">31</ref> .

text.text: However, to our knowledge, no prior study has tested whether behavioral performance on both tasks is related.

A recent meta-analysis reported an overlapping activation cluster in the left hippocampus for both associative and transitive inference 58 , suggesting the recruitment of similar neural regions for both tasks.
text.formatted: A recent meta-analysis reported an overlapping activation cluster in the left hippocampus for both associative and transitive inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">58</ref> , suggesting the recruitment of similar neural regions for both tasks.

text.text: Reverse inference from neural correlates alone should always be taken with caution though 59 , highlighting the need for converging behavioral evidence.
text.formatted: Reverse inference from neural correlates alone should always be taken with caution though <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">59</ref> , highlighting the need for converging behavioral evidence.

text.text: Second, memories of directly learned pair relations benefited both associative and transitive inference success.
The current results do not align with Richmond and Pan's findings 15 , which showed no between-person association between direct memory and associative inference in 3-5year-olds.
text.formatted: The current results do not align with Richmond and Pan's findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">15</ref> , which showed no between-person association between direct memory and associative inference in 3-5year-olds.

text.text: Here, we found that within-person, trial-level analyses revealed a stronger link.
Methodological differences likely explain the discrepancy: Richmond and Pan 15 examined between-person differences, while we analyzed within-person variations on a trial-by-trial level.
Other studies looking at trial-by-trial variations have also shown that generalization is tied to the memory for specific instances in children 12, 60, 61 .
text.formatted: Other studies looking at trial-by-trial variations have also shown that generalization is tied to the memory for specific instances in children <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">60,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">61</ref> .

text.text: For example, memory for character-object pairings increased the likelihood of generalizing which new item that character would select 12, 60 .
text.formatted: For example, memory for character-object pairings increased the likelihood of generalizing which new item that character would select <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">60</ref> .

text.text: In another study that used an associative inference paradigm to investigate knowledge derivation based on overlapping facts, Bauer and San Souci 62 showed that children integrated knowledge more readily when related facts were remembered correctly together.
text.formatted: In another study that used an associative inference paradigm to investigate knowledge derivation based on overlapping facts, Bauer and San Souci <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">62</ref> showed that children integrated knowledge more readily when related facts were remembered correctly together.

text.text: It should be noted, though, that the measure of direct pair memory used here differed between the AI and TI tasks and that other differences in task procedure such as length of learning, learning with or without feedback, and response format (2AFC vs.
3AFC) limit a direct side-by-side comparison.
Nonetheless, the findings indicate that direct memory supports generalization across different inference tasks.
Third, the degree to which direct memory benefits generalization in inference tasks increased with age.
Older children drew on prior experiences more efficiently than young children.
Two observations support this claim.
First, among trials for which directly learned pairs were remembered, younger children were still less likely to infer correctly than their older counterparts.
And second, the increase in probability of inference success between incorrect and correct pair memory was stronger in older compared to younger children.

This suggests that direct memory and inference is more tightly linked among older children, potentially reflecting differential developments of the neural underpinnings of memory and generalization throughout childhood.

Neurocomputational models have proposed that the hippocampal subfields CA3 and dentate gyrus are involved in memory for specific relational details 32, 63 , whereas CA1 is involved in generalization and inference 32, 33 .
text.formatted: Neurocomputational models have proposed that the hippocampal subfields CA3 and dentate gyrus are involved in memory for specific relational details <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">63</ref> , whereas CA1 is involved in generalization and inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">33</ref> .

text.text: These subfields mature at different rates 35, 64, 65 , with CA1 developing earlier than CA3 and DG.
text.formatted: These subfields mature at different rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">64,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">65</ref> , with CA1 developing earlier than CA3 and DG.

text.text: This asynchronous maturation may limit the extent to which these subregions cooperate in early development.
In adults, there is neural evidence of both integrated representations in CA1 and differentiated representations in CA3 and dentate gyrus 66, 67.
text.formatted: In adults, there is neural evidence of both integrated representations in CA1 and differentiated representations in CA3 and dentate gyrus <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">66,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">67</ref>.

text.text: Recent reinforcement learning studies suggest that from late childhood to adulthood, both general and specific representations guide decisions 68 .
text.formatted: Recent reinforcement learning studies suggest that from late childhood to adulthood, both general and specific representations guide decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">68</ref> .

text.text: Thus, it is likely that over development, children become better at forming differentiated representations which are in turn also utilizable for episodic inferences.
Fourth, the weak association between memory and inference in younger children during transitive inference stems from accurate inference despite poor memory for the constituent pairs.

A weak coupling between generalization and memory specificity can result from two types of mismatches: (1) successful generalization despite inaccurate memory specificity (alternative route), or (2) unsuccessful generalization despite accurate memory specificity (knowledge-behavior gap).
In the AI task, these patterns were relatively balanced.

However, in the TI task, successful generalization in the absence of accurate memory was prevalent in younger children, suggesting that they may have relied on a different strategy to solve the task 17 .
text.formatted: However, in the TI task, successful generalization in the absence of accurate memory was prevalent in younger children, suggesting that they may have relied on a different strategy to solve the task <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">17</ref> .

text.text: Employing a computational model revealed that the alternative route involved using individual item values, rather than relational pair memory, to guide choices.
Computational modelling has the potential to provide insights that are hard to derive from behavioral data alone 69 .
text.formatted: Computational modelling has the potential to provide insights that are hard to derive from behavioral data alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">69</ref> .

text.text: In the present case, comparing a reinforcement learning model to a memory model that can in principle both perform transitive inference across age groups revealed important differences. 8-year-old's behavior was best explained by a model that relies on memory for individual pairs and linking them for inference (Pair+). 4-and 6-year-olds' performance were best explained by a reinforcement learning model akin to "functional reasoning" 17, 39 that performs transitive inference without requiring that children explicitly learn the transitive structure.
text.formatted: In the present case, comparing a reinforcement learning model to a memory model that can in principle both perform transitive inference across age groups revealed important differences. 8-year-old's behavior was best explained by a model that relies on memory for individual pairs and linking them for inference (Pair+). 4-and 6-year-olds' performance were best explained by a reinforcement learning model akin to "functional reasoning" <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">39</ref> that performs transitive inference without requiring that children explicitly learn the transitive structure.

text.text: This suggests that different age groups may use strategies with different complexity when performing the same transitive inference task.

However, because 8-year-olds' performance was near ceiling, the findings in this age group should be interpreted cautiously: the Pair+ model appears to account for near-perfect performance, but limited variance restricts potential conclusions.
Model comparison also suggests that part of the 8-year-old age group might be explained by the RL model and, hence, we cannot conclusively disentangle both models.
Similarly, 4-year-olds may in part be explained by Pair0, the model that only learns item pairings and cannot perform inference.
Therefore, it seems that strategies for solving the TI task are more heterogeneous in younger children, in line with similar recent findings in younger participants 70, 71.
text.formatted: Therefore, it seems that strategies for solving the TI task are more heterogeneous in younger children, in line with similar recent findings in younger participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">70,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">71</ref>.

text.text: One might also ask why 8-year-old children are better explained by the pair-level model and, therefore, differ from the item-level strategy that both younger children in the current study as well as adults in a previous study employing this model showed 42 .
text.formatted: One might also ask why 8-year-old children are better explained by the pair-level model and, therefore, differ from the item-level strategy that both younger children in the current study as well as adults in a previous study employing this model showed <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">42</ref> .

text.text: As mentioned above, we are cautious in interpreting this finding due to the ceiling effects and, hence, limited variance in choice behavior to distinguish models.
However, substantial differences between the current study and the study by Ciranka et al. 42 may additionally account for this discrepancy.
text.formatted: However, substantial differences between the current study and the study by Ciranka et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">42</ref> may additionally account for this discrepancy.

text.text: Their task was generally harder, requiring participants to complete a larger number of trials, and was more abstract and not as visual as the task used here.

Moreover, learning the premise pairs and being tested on the transitive pairs was done in an interleaved fashion throughout the entire experiment, and participants had to learn a greater number of items.
The relatively easier paradigm used in the present study may have favored pair-level learning in the oldest age group.
It is still actively debated whether encoding-or retrieval-based mechanisms predominantly support inference (for an extensive review, see 4 ).
text.formatted: It is still actively debated whether encoding-or retrieval-based mechanisms predominantly support inference (for an extensive review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">4</ref> ).

text.text: One prominent theory, integrative encoding, suggests that new information is encoded together with existing memories given overlapping elements 72, 73 .
text.formatted: One prominent theory, integrative encoding, suggests that new information is encoded together with existing memories given overlapping elements <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">72,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">73</ref> .

text.text: In contrast, retrieval-based accounts propose that memory representations are coded individually in an episodic-like way, including their relationship to one another 74 .
text.formatted: In contrast, retrieval-based accounts propose that memory representations are coded individually in an episodic-like way, including their relationship to one another <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">74</ref> .

text.text: These are then retrieved together from partial input by means of pattern completion for generalization 63, 75 .
text.formatted: These are then retrieved together from partial input by means of pattern completion for generalization <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">63,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">75</ref> .

text.text: Assigning values to stimuli and using them to guide future choices can be seen as a type of encoding mechanism, while linking memories of pair relationships at test as a retrieval mechanism.

A recent study that examined whether integrated representations of overlapping events are used to perform associative inference found no evidence for the encoding of such integrated representations in children 76.
text.formatted: A recent study that examined whether integrated representations of overlapping events are used to perform associative inference found no evidence for the encoding of such integrated representations in children <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">76</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, another study investigating associative inference using eye tracking to probe whether memory integration took place, found that only adults showed signs of integration, while children did not 77 .
text.formatted: Similarly, another study investigating associative inference using eye tracking to probe whether memory integration took place, found that only adults showed signs of integration, while children did not <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">77</ref> .

text.text: Relating this to the current study, it is likely that integrated memories were not formed, but that children used separate memories at retrieval in the AI task.

We speculate that this underscores one divergence between the two tasks used here: successful associative inference relies predominantly on retrieval mechanisms, whereas successful transitive inference, at least in 4-and 6year-olds, relies predominantly on an encoding mechanism of associating items with values, bypassing the use of individual memories (also see 78 , for an encoding-based account of transitive inference in adults).
text.formatted: We speculate that this underscores one divergence between the two tasks used here: successful associative inference relies predominantly on retrieval mechanisms, whereas successful transitive inference, at least in 4-and 6year-olds, relies predominantly on an encoding mechanism of associating items with values, bypassing the use of individual memories (also see <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">78</ref> , for an encoding-based account of transitive inference in adults).

text.text: Finally, despite similar age-related trends across all four tasks we used, the mainly inconclusive results from the BF analysis leave the question open whether generalization is a unitary construct or relies on distinct mechanisms.
Age-related increases in performance were observed on nearly all tasks and most consistently from ages 4 to 6.

This task-invariant age pattern corroborates previous findings that used single-task designs in developmental samples: 4-year-olds performed better than chance on both the transitive 20, 22 and associative inference 15 task, while temporal regularity performance did not exceed chance until the age of 6 79 .
text.formatted: This task-invariant age pattern corroborates previous findings that used single-task designs in developmental samples: 4-year-olds performed better than chance on both the transitive <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">22</ref> and associative inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">15</ref> task, while temporal regularity performance did not exceed chance until the age of 6 <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">79</ref> .

text.text: One possibility for the lack of inter-task associations within individual age groups could have been limited task reliability.

However, we found that reliabilities were high across the entire sample and only tended to be lower in 4-yearolds, and even there the influence on the disattenuated correlation was minimal (excluding the negative reliability in the TR task due to chance performance).
Therefore, we ruled out low reliability as reason for not finding strong inter-task correlations.
A different possibility is that our sample size was too small, leaving not enough power to detect a common underlying factor even if it exists.
Lastly, evidence of correlations between tasks were mostly inconclusive, providing no support for the notion of one common factor underlying generalization abilities.

This mirrors recent findings in exploration and risk-taking, where indicators previously thought to capture these constructs do not cohere and rather measure differing aspects of these constructs 80, 81 .
text.formatted: This mirrors recent findings in exploration and risk-taking, where indicators previously thought to capture these constructs do not cohere and rather measure differing aspects of these constructs <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">80,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">81</ref> .

text.text: In the current case, the basis for using these tasks mainly comes from a variety of neuroimaging studies in adults (reviewed in 2 ) and related neurocomputational models [31] [32] [33] suggesting involvement of the hippocampus in rapid generalization.
text.formatted: In the current case, the basis for using these tasks mainly comes from a variety of neuroimaging studies in adults (reviewed in 2 ) and related neurocomputational models <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[31]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[32]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[33]</ref> suggesting involvement of the hippocampus in rapid generalization.

text.text: Direct behavioral evidence supporting a common underlying construct is scarce, though, in both adults and children.
Thus, important differences between tasks indicate that generalization may be more multifaceted than previously assumed.
However, further studies are needed to corroborate these claims.
Several limitations should be noted.
First, task procedures were modified mid-study for the TR and TI tasks.
Although no performance differences were found between procedural versions, small sample sizes may impair confidence in this conclusion.
Second, the study was not designed to support joint computational modelling of transitive and associative inference or any other tasks and, thus, we could not implement parallel models across tasks.
Future work should thus design comparable generalization tasks to allow direct model-based comparisons that is better suited to inform about different mechanisms of generalization.
Third, in addition to the above-mentioned possibilities for the null result, the combination of measures might not have been sensitive enough to capture sufficient variability across tasks.

Having encountered both floor and ceiling effects and substantial drop out from the youngest age group in the CAT task tied with previously reported low reliability in the TR task 82 and in the current 4-year-old sample indicate measurement problems.
text.formatted: Having encountered both floor and ceiling effects and substantial drop out from the youngest age group in the CAT task tied with previously reported low reliability in the TR task <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">82</ref> and in the current 4-year-old sample indicate measurement problems.

text.text: Task difficulty and age-appropriateness may also have varied, obscuring potential inter-task associations.
Finally, the modeling results from 4-year-olds need to be taken with some additional caution.
While our GLMM analysis did not reveal an effect of distance in this age group, the RL model would make this prediction.
Multiple explanations exist for why this is the case.

First, the model simulations in Fig. 6B also do not show a strong distance effect for 4-year-olds even though these are generated by the RL model, which may in part be due to the lower sensitivity to distances in younger children as shown by a larger h parameter (see also Supplementary Fig. S5).
text.formatted: First, the model simulations in Fig. <ref type="figure">6B</ref> also do not show a strong distance effect for 4-year-olds even though these are generated by the RL model, which may in part be due to the lower sensitivity to distances in younger children as shown by a larger h parameter (see also Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure">S5</ref>).

text.text: Second, the potentially larger heterogeneity in the youngest age group could have weakened the effect overall.
Therefore, the GLMM analysis might not have been sensitive enough to detect a distance effect.
Moreover, pseudo-R² shows considerably lower model fit overall.

This is most likely due to children responding more variably, indicated by greater estimates for the temperature parameter titem, thus limiting the interpretation that this is the only underlying model for their behavior.
In sum, the present results highlight early to middle childhood as an important period for the development of generalization capacities.
However, whether generalization is a unitary process or not remains an open question: the four tasks may also rely on distinct cognitive and, potentially, neural mechanisms.

As we found inconclusive evidence, a closer examination of task designs and the application of multi-indicator approaches will be crucial for understanding to which degree generalization is multifaceted across development.

Further, investigating associative and transitive inference we find consistency in that children's inference is tied to memories for the underlying information and that this association becomes stronger with age.
This suggests a maturational process of brain regions responsible for these processes working more closely together later in development.
Moreover, the modeling results suggest that younger children's success in transitive inference may rather arise from item-value-based rather than pair-memory-based strategies.

Applying computational models across multiple generalization tasks within individuals will be fruitful to determine if generalization is task-specific across ontogeny and to which degree it still reflects a unified process.

Together, the present findings highlight the need to clarify whether generalization capacities develop through single or multiple developmental pathways driven by emerging cognitive prerequisites.    S8).

Among 8-yearolds, the best-fitting model (Pair+) uses pairwise item associations to infer transitive relations-a logical benchmark for children who are near ceiling performance.

text.formatted: A) Learning Phase: Children learned the relationship between five jumpers across individual premise (A<B, B<C, C<D, D<E).

text.text: The first learning phase continued until children reached 80% accuracy on each pair.

In the second learning phase, premise pairs were presented in an intermixed order, and learning continued until children either selected the correct jumper on six consecutive trials per pair or achieved 80% accuracy per pair.
Different learning phases are denoted by the circled numbers on the left.

B) Test Phase: In the 2AFC task, children were probed on their memory for premise pairs seen during learning as well as inferred the relationships between non-adjacent, transitive pairs (e.g., BD), both without corrective feedback.
